text: Approximately 700 women across the United States die each year as a result of pregnancy or pregnancy-related complications.
Non-Hispanic Black women experience maternal deaths at a rate three to four times that of non-Hispanic White women.
The Nine Committees estimated that over 60% of pregnancy-related deaths were preventable.
The most common contributing factors were patient/family factors, followed by provider and systems-of-care factors.
Cardiovascular and coronary conditions, hemorrhage, and infection accounted for nearly half of pregnancy-related deaths.
Mental health conditions were a leading underlying cause of death among non-Hispanic White women.
Prenatal care providers should screen all patients for substance use disorders at their first prenatal visit.
Improve communication between prenatal care providers, mental health providers, and primary care providers.
Promote universal screening prenatally and continued in the postpartum period for mental health conditions.
Establish co-prescribing methods for opioid prescriptions, offering naloxone together with prescribed opioids.
A lack of coordination between providers in patient management contributed to many preventable deaths.
Committees recommended adopting levels of maternal care and enforcing policies related to obstetric hemorrhage.
